# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–6 (Complete and Final – Updated 76)

## Setting and Time
- **Period**: Spring through late August of first year; Christmas/New Year period; nearly three weeks into new year (1832) just after Lords threw out Reform Bill; summer and autumn of first year; winter of first year; Vauxhall evening during spring of first year; spring of second year; summer of second year (current narrative point); narrative extends into future years; present day with Fred and Mary at Stone Court in white-haired placidity
- **Primary Locations**: Middlemarch, Lowick, Grange, Freshitt, Mirecombe, Salwick, Quenwick, Fenmere, Bryngate, Chalky Flats, Gulton, Highbury, Cheltenham, Tipton, Yoddrell's farm, Frick, Miremere, Riverston, Quallingham, Halsell Wood, Loamford, Brassing, Stone Court, Coldcombe, St. Peter's Place, Lowick Gate, Shrubs, Dunholt, Yorkshire, Staveton, Bilkley, Harrowgate, Melspring, Wilhaven, Salford, Chiswick Mall, Hammersmith, Soho, Thames, England, Oxford, Chiswick Church, Buxton, Kensington turnpike, Russell Square, London, Southampton Row, Vauxhall, Exeter 'Change, India (Boggley Wollah, Ramgunge, Budgebudge, Calcutta, Dumdum), Forty Thieves theatre, King's 14th regiment post, Highbury Barn, Covent Garden Market, Doctor Swishtail's Seminary, Bedford tavern, Thames Street (City), Royal Gardens, Quenwick, Wilhaven, St. George's Hanover Square, Lambeth Palace, Cheltenham, Great Gaunt Street, Queen's Crawley (Hants), Mudbury, Gaunt Square, Mansion House, Oxford Street, Swallow Street, Cambridge, Leakington, Squashmore, Bethesda Chapel Liverpool, Naples, Paris, Eton, Pumpernickel, Strasburg, Crawley parish, Yarlton, Quashimaboo, Mirecombe, Fuddleston, Roxby, Wapshot Hall, Christchurch, Rectory House, Hampshire, Chiswick, Coldcombe, Huddleston, Cocoa-Tree, Woolwich, hill farms of Coldcombe, Humdrum Hall, Wattier's, Chatham, Horse Guards, Carlton House, St. Kitt's, Opera, Prince Regent locations
- **Narrative Presence**: Narrator warns Vanity Fair is "a very vain, wicked, foolish place, full of all sorts of humbugs and falsenesses and pretensions"; observes human hearts and self-deceptions with ironic sympathy; notes merit of describing modest hearts honestly despite grammar or meter; refuses to judge the selfish but notes their nature

## Main Characters

**Dorothea and Will Ladislaw (Married)**
- Married with infant son; established pattern of two yearly visits to Grange; Dorothea's life mixed result of young, noble impulse

**Mary Garth and Fred Garth (Married)**
- Inhabit Stone Court in white-haired placidity; Fred becomes distinguished county farmer with work on "Cultivation of Green Crops and the Economy of Cattle-Feeding"; three boys only, youngest resembles grandfather

**Rebecca Sharp (Miss Becky)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Background**: Age nineteen; father artist/drawing teacher at Miss Pinkerton's academy (clever, prone to debt/taverns, beat wife/daughter when drunk, died after third delirium tremens); mother French opera-girl; claims descent from Entrechats family of Gascony
- **Education**: Pupil of Miss Pinkerton at Chiswick; received out of charity; Miss Pinkerton notes talents considerable, principles hitherto correct
- **Appearance**: Small, slight, pale, sandy-haired with large odd attractive eyes; white slender fingers
- **Accomplishments**: Speaks French with purity and Parisian accent; skilled musician, linguist, artist; proficient in globes; studied under Signor Clementi on piano
- **Character**: Determined, never blushed since age eight; capable of calculated charm; observant; thinks "I might go farther, and fare worse"; cares nothing for pupils
- **Joseph Sedley Romance Campaign**: Upon learning of his wealth, determined to marry him; won over entire household; Joseph began eloquent speech "O Miss Sharp, how--" but stopped when music ended; at Vauxhall took Jos's arm, lost in solitary walk; during inebriation Jos shouted "Stop, my dearest diddle-diddle-darling"; George Osborne pushed Jos back; Jos never came; household (except Amelia) turned against Rebecca; Blenkinsop reported her reading Mrs. Sedley's letters and accessing trinket boxes; Pinner suspected her of taking Amelia's white ribbing; received purse from Mr. Sedley
- **Governess at Queen's Crawley**: As governess to Rose and Violet; treats Lady Crawley with cool respect; reads with pupils delightful works (Dr. Smollett, Henry Fielding, Monsieur Crebillon, Voltaire, "Humphrey Clinker," French plays); plays backgammon with Sir Pitt; shows respectful obedience to Mr. Pitt Crawley, consults him on French passages, affects tears at his discourses; has "come round" everybody; writes Sir Pitt's letters, does his business, manages accounts; has upper hand of whole house—Lady Crawley, Mr. Pitt Crawley, the girls and all
- **Relationship with Miss Crawley**: Upon Miss Crawley's arrival at Hall, Rebecca's fascinations have won her heart; during accustomed drive to Mudbury, Miss Crawley ordered "that little governess" should accompany her; before return, Rebecca made conquest of her, made her laugh four times, amused her during journey; Miss Crawley now demands Rebecca sit at table during dinners of ceremony despite governess status; declared "I insist upon Miss Sharp appearing. Let Lady Crawley remain upstairs"; when Sir Huddleston prepared to sit by Miss Crawley at dinner, old lady cried "Becky Sharp! Miss Sharp! Come you and sit by me and amuse me"; after parties, Miss Crawley says "Come to my dressing room, Becky, and let us abuse the company"—pair mock Sir Huddleston's wheezing, Sir Giles Wapshot's loud soup-imbibing, Lady Wapshot's left-eye wink; Becky caricatures company and tears to tatters Misses Wapshot's toilettes and Lady Fuddleston's yellow hat to infinite amusement; Miss Crawley now orders Rawdon Crawley should lead her in to dinner every day and Becky should follow with cushion (or Becky's arm and Rawdon with pillow); Miss Crawley declares "We're the only three Christians in the county, my love"
- **Relationship with Rawdon Crawley**: Captain Rawdon has distinguished her many times before; met her in half-score of walks, half-hundred of corridors and passages; hung over her piano twenty times of an evening (Lady Crawley now upstairs ill, nobody heeds her) as Miss Sharp sang; written her notes (blundering dragoon's spelling); when he put first note in leaves of song she was singing, Rebecca took it up daintily, waved it like cocked hat, advanced to enemy, popped note into fire, made very low curtsey, returned to place, sang more merrily than ever; Rebecca has NOT given altogether accurate account of their interactions when writing to friend Amelia; Rawdon has declined entertainments at Fuddleston, would not dine with mess at Mudbury; his great pleasure is to stroll over to Crawley Rectory with Miss Crawley; Miss Crawley also comes; children come with Miss Sharp; evening walks over Rectory fields return through dark plantation and checkered avenue to Queen's Crawley charming in moonlight for "two such lovers of the picturesque as the Captain and Miss Rebecca"; at river crossing in Gulton, Rebecca tastes cigar "in prettiest way possible," gives little puff and scream and giggle, restores delicacy to Captain who twirls moustache; Old Sir Pitt from study-window espied pair so occupied with cigar, with dreadful oaths swore if not for Miss Crawley he'd bundle Rawdon out of doors like rogue
- **Current Status**: Has successfully conquered entire Crawley household including Miss Crawley; Rawdon increasingly attached to her; Miss Crawley calls her "little paragon—positively a little jewel—You have more brains than half the shire"; Miss Crawley says "if merit had its reward you ought to be a Duchess"; treats Rebecca as equal in every respect while making her run errands, execute millinery, read her to sleep with French novels every night

**George Osborne** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Background**: Handsome brother of Amelia Sedley; believed by society to be infatuated with Amelia
- **Character and Behavior**: Jolly sociable fellow; excellent in all games of skill; proficient at billiards
- **Actual Behavior**: Leaves home every morning and dines abroad six days a week, ostensibly with Amelia; however, NOT always with Amelia despite world supposing him at her feet; on more occasions than one, when Captain Dobbin calls seeking him, Miss Osborne points to opposite side of square and says he must be at Sedleys', "WE never see him from morning till night"; frequently plays billiards with Captain Cannon in Swallow Street while Amelia awaits him; has convinced Misses Osborne and their governess that he is making romantic sacrifice and acting with generous resignation in pursuing Amelia; pushed Jos back at Vauxhall during Joseph's inebriated declarations to Rebecca
- **Financial Status**: Receives allowance and mingled in society; considered great ornament to every society
- **Letters**: Short and soldierlike; infrequent

**Amelia Sedley** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Background**: Rebecca's former schoolfriend at Chiswick; came out into world and spurned by discriminating sex despite having many friends at school and being beloved there
- **Character and Appearance**: Small, modest, unaffected young creature; tender heart; timid; not "heroine" of bold type; sweet modest little soul like violet rather than sunflower; fragrant and blooming tenderly in quiet shady places
- **Relationship with George Osborne**: Became object of his attentions; Amelia confirmed him as engaged to her when speaking to young Bullock; believed deeply in George; innocent and trusting; when George runs errands and dines abroad, Amelia waits believing him at Horse Guards, Chatham with regiment, or obliged to see friends and mingle in society; assumes he is too tired to write long letters when with regiment
- **Behavior**: Leaves home every morning and dines abroad six days week; has been told George is at Sedleys' apron-strings but actually rarely there; neglected twelve dear friends at Chiswick most cruelly; has single subject to think about; Miss Saltire too cold for confidante; couldn't bring herself to confide in Miss Swartz, woolly-haired heiress from St. Kitt's; made confidante of little Laura Martin (home for holidays); promised Laura would live with her when married; gave Laura information regarding passion of love; after three days of absence, put on bonnet and invaded Osborne house; told Misses Osborne she only came to see dear friends; was perfectly stupid and awkward; went away sadly; when Captain Dobbin called at Sedley house seeking George, sat near drawing-room window with "rather sad wistful face"; after trifling stupid talk, asked Captain Dobbin if regiment ordered abroad and if he'd seen Mr. Osborne that day; when Dobbin offered to fetch George, gave his hand kindly and gratefully; waited but George never came
- **Letters to George**: Extraordinarily long and passionate; filled sheets of large paper crossed with astonishing perverseness; wrote whole pages of poetry-books without pity; underlined words and passages with frantic emphasis; repetitive; doubtful grammar sometimes; took liberties with metre in verses; usual tokens of her emotional condition evident throughout
- **Emotional State**: Heart beating and longing and trusting all day; only feeling: "when will he come?"; only thought to sleep and wake upon; suffered three days of absence with evident distress; eyes filled with tears when speaking to Osborne sisters; kept packet of George's letters in chamber
- **Current Status**: Loves George completely and trustingly; does not doubt him; neglected by parents who do not keep her heart from beating fast

**Captain Dobbin** [CHARACTER]
- **Character and Manner**: Friend of George Osborne; attentive and kind; enjoys military stories and inquiries about health; consummate man of world able to turn conversation smoothly
- **Behavior and Knowledge**: Calls to look for George at Osborne house; Miss Osborne very attentive to him; when Miss Osborne points to opposite side of square saying George must be at Sedleys', Dobbin laughs in "rather absurd constrained manner"; had been calling at Mr. Sedley's house already on pretence of seeing George; George wasn't there, only Amelia; after trifling talk with Amelia, offered to fetch George; crossed square but George never came; does not inform young ladies of his knowledge of Amelia's situation
- **Status**: Blushed and looked awkward when remembering his visits to Sedley house

**Sir Pitt Crawley, Baronet** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Financial History**: Estate never recovered from heavy fine on Walpole Crawley (first baronet); cellars not burgundy-filled, kennels not hound-filled
- **Character and Behavior**: Old, stumpy, short, vulgar, very dirty man in old clothes and shabby gaiters; shining bald head, leering red face, twinkling grey eyes, perpetually grinning; country accent; swears great deal; could not spell and did not care to read
- **Financial Practices**: Almost invincible repugnance to paying anybody; said "What's the good of being in Parliament if you must pay your debts?"
- **Parliamentary Position**: High sheriff; has higher place in Vanity Fair than most brilliant genius or spotless virtue
- **Current Status**: Arranges dinners of ceremony with neighbouring baronets; with Miss Crawley's intervention, agreed young people of both families should visit each other frequently; taking pipe and beer, talking to John Horrocks about livestock

**Mr. Pitt Crawley (Eldest Son)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Character and Manner**: Pale, thin, ugly, silent; thin legs, no chest; hay-coloured whiskers; in full dress pompous as undertaker; very earnest; high-bred propriety
- **Career**: Studied ancient and modern orators with assiduity; became Private Secretary to Lord Binkie; appointed Attache to Legation at Pumpernickel; remained ten years Attache after Lord Binkie's demise; exceedingly proud of French language skills; turned country gentleman; wrote pamphlet on Malt; took strong part in Negro Emancipation; became friend of Mr. Wilberforce; gave speech at Quashimaboo-Aid Society
- **Activities**: In London during Parliament, in May for religious meetings; in country as magistrate; subjected servants to devotional exercises; patronized Independent meeting-house in Crawley parish; criticizes Rebecca's backgammon-playing as godless
- **Political Ambition**: Very earnest old gentleman should yield up Parliament place; Sir Pitt constantly refuses; both too prudent to give up fifteen hundred a year

**Rawdon Crawley (Younger Son)** [CHARACTER]
- **Background**: From Sir Pitt's first marriage; at Eton licked brother Pitt violently
- **Character and Lifestyle**: Perfect celebrated "blood," or dandy about town; expert in boxing, rat-hunting, fives court, four-in-hand driving; belonged to household troops around Prince Regent; fought three bloody duels; great contempt for Queen's Crawley; seldom came except when aunt Miss Crawley paid annual visit; intellect and conversation brilliant and becoming to heavy young dragoon
- **Financial Status**: Over head and ears in debt; known gambler, drunkard, profligate; shot Captain Marker in duel; robbed young Lord Dovedale at Cocoa-Tree; crossed fight between Bill Soames and Cheshire Trump by which Rector lost forty pounds; has women entanglements; adored in his regiment; all young men at Wattier's and Cocoa-Tree swear by him; "delightfully wicked," "has hit a man, and shot an injured father through the hat"
- **Relationship with Miss Crawley**: Almost adopted him; disliked elder nephew Mr. Pitt exceedingly, despised him as milksop; always paid his debts after duels; signified intention of leaving inheritance between Rawdon and family at Rectory; per Rector's information, has him down in will for fifty thousand pounds
- **Relationship with Rebecca**: See Rebecca Sharp section; has given up hunting, declined entertainments; great pleasure strolling to Crawley Rectory; evening walks with Rebecca charming in moonlight; increasingly attached to her; Miss Crawley facilitates their proximity
- **Current Status**: Very large young dandy, six feet high, speaks with great voice, swears greatly; very generous of his money; now ordered by Miss Crawley to lead her in to dinner every day; considered by Miss Crawley one of "only three Christians in the county"

**Miss Crawley (Unmarried Half-Sister)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Background and Character**: Inherited large fortune from mother; old lady, silly and romantic; disliked Mr. Pitt exceedingly; became very attached to Rawdon as boy
- **Financial Position**: Possesses seventy thousand pounds in five per cents; signified intention of leaving inheritance between Rawdon and family at Rectory (Rector claims Rawdon designated for fifty thousand pounds, thirty to divide among others); Rector speculates she drops in year
- **Views on Romance**: "What is birth, my dear!" says to Rebecca; compares Pitt, Huddlestons, Bute unfavorably to Rebecca's intelligence and breeding; considers Rebecca equal in every respect; calls her "little paragon—positively a little jewel"; says Rebecca has more brains than half the shire; if merit had reward Rebecca ought to be Duchess; adores imprudent matches; says "What I like best, is for a nobleman to marry a miller's daughter, as Lord Flowerdale did--it makes all the women so angry"; wishes great man would run away with Rebecca; approves of Lord Nelson's character for going to deuce for woman; recent scandal: Ensign Shafton ran away with Lady Barbara Fitzurse, Earl of Bruin's daughter; Vere Vane left home for Mrs. Rougemont actress age sixty-five; drank cherry-brandy after dinner and took curacao with coffee
- **Current Status**: Mediatrix between brothers; established agreement that young people visit frequently; insists Rebecca sit at dinners, be personal companion, mock society with her; declares Rebecca, Rawdon, and herself "only three Christians in the county"; orders Rawdon lead her in to dinner, Rebecca follow with cushion; demands Rebecca at table during ceremony dinners; says "Come to my dressing room, Becky, and let us abuse the company"

**Mrs. Bute Crawley (Rector's Wife)**
- **Background**: Amiable former pupil of Miss Pinkerton, sprightly accomplished Miss Martha MacTavish in youth
- **Character and Appearance**: Little, black-faced old woman in turban, crooked, very twinkling eyes
- **Recent Actions**: Initially reported Rebecca as artful hussy with dreadful designs; wrote to Miss Pinkerton inquiring about Rebecca; now suddenly taken great fancy to Rebecca; invited girls to Rectory; paid Rebecca compliments; complimented Rebecca and Rawdon's country-dance steps (unprecedented honor from proud woman); became very fond of each other's society with Rawdon
- **Plan**: PLAN (active, not fully executed) hopes to secure Rebecca as piano professor for her children using Rebecca's talents; welcomes young lady to Rectory and Rawdon, her husband's rival in Miss Crawley's five per cents

**Reverend Bute Crawley (Rector, Uncle to Mr. Pitt)**
- **Appearance and Character**: Tall, stately, jolly, shovel-hatted man; far more popular in county than Baronet brother; at college pulled stroke-oar in Christchurch boat; thrashed bruisers; carried boxing taste into private life
- **Social Activity**: Attends every fight, race, coursing match, regatta, ball, election, dinner within twenty miles; seen at Fuddleston, Roxby, Wapshot Hall with great county lords; had fine voice; rode to hounds in pepper-and-salt frock; one of best fishermen in county
- **Financial Concerns**: Thinking about debts; son Jim at College, Frank at Woolwich; four daughters no beauties, would not have penny but expected legacy from aunt; deeply resentful of Rawdon's position in Miss Crawley's will; claims Rawdon has robbed him and his of best part of Miss Crawley's fortune; speculates Miss Crawley drops in year, will leave only thirty thousand to divide
- **Recent Actions**: Asked why Rawdon Crawley was invited to dine; expressed contempt for Rawdon as gambler, drunkard, profligate, murderer character; claimed Rawdon "has got every vice except hypocrisy" (unlike brother); vehemently refused to meet Rawdon Crawley, agreed to visit Sir Huddleston Fuddleston instead, offered to run his greyhound Lancelot in race for fifty pounds; after being called intoxicated by wife, promised to visit Sir Huddleston Fuddleston on Saturday and return in time for Sunday church

**Other Characters and Information**
- **Miss Pinkerton**: Headmistress at Chiswick; received letter from Mrs. Bute Crawley; responded noting Rebecca's talents considerable, principles hitherto correct
- **Young Bullock**: Of firm Hulker, Bullock & Co., Bankers, Lombard Street; had been making up to Miss Maria Sedley last two seasons; asked Amelia to dance cotillon; Amelia told him she was engaged to George
- **Joseph Sedley**: Away being besieged by an Irish widow at Cheltenham
- **Old Sedley (Amelia's father)**: Graver of late; City affairs absorb him; does not seem to notice Amelia's situation
- **Mrs. Sedley (Amelia's mother)**: Of easy and uninquisitive nature; not jealous
- **Misses Osborne and their governess**: Stare after Amelia when she leaves; wonder what George could see in her; excellent critics of Cashmere shawls and pink satin slips; consider Rebecca a fade and insipid correspondent; unaware of George's actual whereabouts when told he is at Sedleys'
- **Other Stenworth family members**: Orrine Stenworth (packed single trunk and moved from Gulton to Coldcombe); Nynelle Stenworth (walked long way round to avoid muddy square; remarked on river being up in spring; complained of salt price); Orbin Stenworth (followed to Coldcombe within the month); Rira Stenworth (told Feena she looked tired); Rozek, Halan, Feena (unnamed speakers in background observations)
- **Other background figures**: Captain Cannon (plays billiards with George), Miss Saltire, Miss Swartz (woolly-haired heiress from St. Kitt's), Laura Martin (little friend Amelia confided in), Mrs. Firkin, Sir Huddleston Fuddleston, Sir Giles Wapshot, Lady Wapshot, Misses Wapshot, Lady Fuddleston, John Horrocks, Ensign Shafton, Lady Barbara Fitzurse, Vere Vane, Mrs. Rougemont, Lord Nelson, Lord Flowerdale, Lord Binkie, Mr. Wilberforce

## Critical Facts and Status
- Parliamentary seat at Queen's Crawley worth fifteen hundred a year; family estate much embarrassed
- Rebecca has successfully conquered entire Queen's Crawley household and Miss Crawley's favor within summer of second year
- Rawdon increasingly attached to Rebecca; their evening walks charming in moonlight; Miss Crawley facilitates their proximity
- Miss Crawley's seventy-thousand-pound inheritance disputed; Rector claims Rawdon designated for fifty thousand pounds, thirty to divide among others
- Mrs. Bute Crawley's plan to secure Rebecca as piano professor for her children not yet fully executed but becoming operative
- George Osborne's actual behavior contradicts public belief in his devotion to Amelia; he frequents billiard halls and plays rather than visits her
- Amelia's innocent love is unaware of George's actual preoccupations; she trusts completely and waits faithfully, writing passionate lengthy letters
- Captain Dobbin aware of discrepancy between George's claimed whereabouts and actual location; maintains discretion
